output.framing: The proposal: release notes should be derived from the merged change record rather than written after the fact, so the notes cannot drift from what actually shipped; the author would rather adopt an established convention or tool than invent a format, and has not chosen either yet. A repo check supports exploring this now: Nexus has no release tags and no changelog today, so there is nothing to retrofit; the merge history mixes three conventions (bare summaries, lower-case prefixes such as 'docs:', and 'HARN-<n>:' keys) with conventional merge-commit lines, and no written commit or PR-title convention exists in the project docs. One observation that seems to bear on the idea: every merged change here is tied to a Jira task whose key, summary and description are already normalized and human-written, and PR titles tend to carry that key — so the richest record of intent may already exist before the merge. Also worth naming, without it being a defect: if notes are derived strictly from the merge record with no later writing at all, they will report what changed but rarely why it mattered; whether the notes are a faithful enumeration or need a light judgment layer is a choice the refinement can settle.
questions: Who reads these notes and what decision or check do they support — Nexus's own operators and contributors, or the users of projects Nexus manages? That shapes how much of the Jira context belongs in a release note.

What precisely is 'the merged change record' for one release: pull request titles and descriptions, commit subjects, the Jira tasks those changes completed, or a combination with a stated precedence? Today's data suggests the Jira summary is the most normalized human text available.

Where and when should the notes appear — in the repository at release time, attached to a version or tag, or published somewhere else? And should anything still be written by hand at any point, or is the intent that the release step is fully mechanical?

The author's premise is written-afterwards notes that drift; existing tools split into two families — some (Conventional Commits plus generators) demand a strict machine-readable convention, others (Changesets, release-drafter) capture a human summary at merge time and assemble the notes automatically. Which trade-off fits better: tightening future convention, or drawing on the task record already produced by the workflow?

output.contribution: Two mature families already do what this idea describes, so nothing has to be invented. (1) Merge-time note artifacts assembled at release: towncrier (used by pip, pytest, Twisted, attrs), Changesets and Changie write a small human entry per change and produce the release notes mechanically. (2) Derivation from the record that already exists: git-cliff can map irregular subjects to categories with regex parsers, GitLab reads a `Changelog:` trailer on the commit, GitHub's built-in generator categorizes merged PRs by label via `.github/release.yml`, and Release Drafter does the same with templates and a PR-time check action. Reader-facing formats also already exist and interlock: Keep a Changelog, the stricter Common Changelog, Conventional Commits types, GitLab's trailer values (which coincide with Keep a Changelog categories). Two discoveries bear directly on the editor's 'what vs why' observation: release-please documents a post-merge wording override (edit the merged PR body with a `BEGIN_COMMIT_OVERRIDE` block and the next run uses that text for release notes — documented for squash merges), and Jira versions are a first-class release boundary (fixVersion searches, `releasedVersions()`), which this repo's HARN-keyed titles could join against. Project facts: there are no tags, no changelog and no release step today (nothing to retrofit), and the merged record mixes merge commits, squash merges, key-prefixed subjects and bare or lower-case-prefixed subjects, with no written commit convention. Limitation: Tavily search quota was exhausted and several search engines refused automated access, so this report rests on direct retrieval of the primary sources listed below.
findings: Project fact (worktree, 2026-09-28): there is no release boundary to derive from yet — `git tag` is empty, no CHANGELOG file exists in the tree, .github/workflows/ci.yml only validates (`npm ci`, `npm run validate`, `npm run smoke:help`), package.json is private at 0.1.0 with no release script, and docs/high-level-architecture.md, docs/task-engine/actions/deliver.md and docs/task-engine/actions/complete-task.md describe no version, tag or release step. The 'nothing to retrofit' reading holds; the idea would also introduce a release boundary the project does not have.

Project fact (git history inspection of the last 80 commits): the merged change record is mixed — about 12 'Merge pull request #N …' merge commits (PR number and branch name, no task key), about 27 subject lines ending '(#N)' (squash merges), about 13 subjects prefixed 'HARN-<n>: ', and about 28 with neither marker (bare summaries such as 'Keep idea dialogue and feedback plain', plus lower-case prefixes such as 'docs:' and 'config:'). Merge commits and squash merges therefore do not carry identical identifying data, which matters to any strict parser.

Project fact: no written commit or PR-title convention appears in docs/agent-runtime/development-role.md (it only requires the implementation to be committed on the supplied branch), and the provider contracts describe what Nexus can read — issue data, comments, field changes and transitions (docs/adapters/jira.md); PR identity, head/base/state and merge revision (docs/adapters/github.md) — not note text.

External fact (Conventional Commits 1.0.0): a lightweight convention layered on commit messages in which `fix` and `feat` correlate with PATCH and MINOR and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer (or `!`) correlates with MAJOR; types other than `feat`/`fix` are allowed, and body and footer sections can carry additional context. The spec's stated purpose is an explicit history that makes it easier to write automated tools on top of.

External fact (Keep a Changelog 1.1.0): a changelog is defined as 'a curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each version'; guiding principles state 'changelogs are for humans, not machines'; and 'commit log diffs' are listed under bad practices because they are 'full of noise' and 'obscure titles'. The same page observes that when software changes, people want to know why and how. Read as a caution about raw commit feeds and as a brief for reader-facing text, not as a verdict on derivation.

External fact (Common Changelog): a stricter, human-facing subset of Keep a Changelog whose prerequisites include one git tag per released version and adherence to Semantic Versioning; entries must be self-describing imperative one-liners, must reference relevant commits and should reference tickets or pull requests when available, list authors, put breaking changes first, and the entry for a new version should be committed before the tag is created.

External fact (GitHub, vendor docs): built-in automatically generated release notes list merged pull requests, the release's contributors and a link to a full changelog; categories and exclusions (labels, authors) are configured in `.github/release.yml`, and a catch-all category can absorb everything else. This is the lowest-effort member of the 'derive from what is already there' family, and its category scheme can be reused by other generators.

External fact (Release Drafter): drafts the next release notes as pull requests are merged; categories come from labels or title conditions; templates expose `$TITLE`, `$NUMBER`, `$AUTHORS`; version-resolver categories influence the next version; an Autolabeler action adds labels, and a read-only Check PR action validates a PR against the category rules — so the categorization decision can be enforced at PR time while the note text stays derived from the merged record.

External fact (GitLab changelogs): generated from commit titles plus Git trailers; a commit is included only if it carries a `Changelog:` trailer, whose values are `added`, `fixed`, `changed`, `deprecated`, `removed`, `security`, `performance`, `other`; output is grouped by that category, can include merge-request links and commit authors, is template-customizable, and is produced over a commit or tag range via API or `glab changelog generate`. The trailer values coincide with the Keep a Changelog categories.

External fact (Git): key/value trailers are a native mechanism (`git interpret-trailers`, as used by `Signed-off-by`), so a trailer-based convention rides on existing git tooling rather than introducing a new artifact format.

External fact (git-cliff): generates changelogs from git history using conventional commits 'as well as regex-powered custom parsers', with a customizable template and configuration file. The custom parsers are what makes it a candidate for this repo's mixed conventions; I did not verify its provider-API enrichment, so no claim is made about it.

External fact (release-please): parses Conventional Commits and opens a release PR that updates the changelog and tags on merge, and it lets one commit represent several changes through footers. Most relevant here: after a PR merges, editing the PR body to include a `BEGIN_COMMIT_OVERRIDE … END_COMMIT_OVERRIDE` block makes the next run use that text instead of the merged commit message for release notes, documented as working with squash-merge and not with plain merges. This is a shipped precedent for 'derived by default, human wording allowed after merge'.

External fact (semantic-release, Cocogitto, commitlint/commitizen): a second family derives version and notes fully mechanically from a formalized convention and enforces it through CI, hooks or a bot. semantic-release's README states it uses commit messages to determine consumer impact, defaults to the Angular commit convention, and recommends commitizen or commitlint to keep messages valid; Cocogitto advertises conventional compliance, automatic version bumps and changelog generation with GitHub enforcement. The cost is a durable change to how every change is described.

External fact (towncrier; used by pip, pytest, Twisted, attrs): news fragments named `<issue-id>.<type>` (feature, bugfix, doc, removal, misc) are written per change and assembled at release; `misc` fragments are recorded but not published; `towncrier build --draft` previews the result. Its philosophy is stated as 'towncrier delivers the news which is convenient to those that hear it, not those that write it', and it 'works best in a development system where all merges involve closing an issue' — directly resonant with a key-per-change workflow.

External fact (Changesets and Changie): the fragment family deliberately separates notes from commit history. A changeset holds a semver version type plus changelog text, written by the person making the contribution at contribution time; the version command consumes them and writes changelog entries, with a recommended review pass, and Changesets advises against blocking contributions that need no changeset. Changie's stated goals are 'separate your changelog from commit messages without conflicts' and 'track changes while you work while the knowledge is fresh', with a GitHub Action available.

External fact (Atlassian Jira): versions are a first-class release boundary — JQL supports `fixVersion` searches and functions such as `earliestUnreleasedVersion()`, `latestReleasedVersion()`, `releasedVersions()` and `unreleasedVersions()`, with version ordering managed on the Releases page. This makes 'everything that shipped in release X' a supported query against the task record that already exists for every change here; correctness depends on version hygiene in Jira.

External evidence (Tian et al., 'What Makes a Good Commit Message?', ICSE 2022, DOI 10.1145/3510003.3510205; arXiv:2202.02974): commit messages are described as the 'audit trail' by which developers understand how a project's source changed — and why; in a sample of almost 1,600 messages from five highly active open-source projects the authors report that roughly 44% could be improved. Read as support for the idea's premise that a faithful record matters, together with a caution that raw record text is often not reader-ready.

Research limitation: Tavily reported its monthly keyless search quota exhausted, and other routes (DuckDuckGo HTML and lite, Mojeek, Brave, Ecosia) refused automated access; Semantic Scholar initially rate-limited. The findings above therefore come from direct retrieval of the primary pages listed in sources plus Crossref/Semantic Scholar lookups for the paper. No broad third-party survey of release-note tooling was possible, so the absence of a tool here is not evidence that none exists.
options: Possibility — capture the note when the change is made (fragment family): towncrier, Changesets or Changie each write a small human entry, with its category, alongside the change, and the release step assembles them. Towncrier's issue-keyed fragment names line up with a key-per-change workflow, and Changesets/Changie exist specifically to keep notes out of the commit log; the possible cost is one extra artifact per change to write and review.

Possibility — derive from the record that already exists, with tolerant parsing: git-cliff's regex parsers and templates, GitLab's `Changelog:` trailer, GitHub's `.github/release.yml` label categories, or Release Drafter's label/title categories would read the merge record without a new per-change artifact; quality would be bounded by whatever the record currently carries.

Possibility — tighten the convention and derive everything: Conventional Commits plus release-please or semantic-release, with commitlint, commitizen or Cocogitto enforcing the convention, would derive notes and versions together; it is the largest behavioural change because every future message must follow the convention.

Possibility — make the Jira task record the entry text: assemble notes from the issues in a Jira version (fixVersion or releasedVersions), using the issue summary as the entry and the key as the link, with the merged record deciding membership rather than wording. Considerations to weigh: summaries are written for planning rather than for readers, and the query is only as good as version assignment in the Jira project.

Possibility — derive by default and allow a late wording fix: release-please's documented PR-body override, or the review-and-tweak step Changesets recommends at version time, gives the 'why' a place to be written after the change is understood without abandoning derivation as the source of the notes.

Possibility — adopt an existing reader-facing format rather than inventing one: Keep a Changelog's six categories, Common Changelog's stricter entry rules (imperative one-liners with commit/PR/ticket references and authors), Conventional Commits types as sections, GitLab's trailer values, or GitHub's release categories; several of these are designed to interlock with one another.

Possibility — name the release boundary as part of the idea, since 'the notes for a release' presumes one: a git tag (GitLab and Common Changelog both key generation off tags) or a Jira version (already a supported boundary) are two candidate homes for it. This can stay an open idea-level choice of where the boundary lives, without settling the mechanism now.

output.contribution: Pursue, with two qualifications. The idea sits with Nexus's own principles — 'Observable' (preserve enough evidence to understand what changed and why) and 'deterministic where simple and reliable' (derive in ordinary software rather than re-narrate by hand) — and it proposes to change an absence, not an enduring choice: this repo has no release boundary and no notes artifact, and nothing in the vision privileges hand-written release prose. Two facts should temper the framing: 'each release' has no anchor today (no tags, version 0.1.0, CI-only workflow), and 'the merged change record' is really three records of unequal quality (mixed commit subjects, PR metadata, Jira tasks), so which one supplies the prose is the substantive choice. The author's stated preference for adopting an existing convention or tool matches the vision's 'use existing agents, tools and services where they meet the need'. One correction to the framing: only 63 of 233 commit subjects carry a HARN key, so Jira does not cover every merged change.
output.fit: Enduring purpose (docs/LONG_TERM_VISION.md): turn intent into verified outcomes, remain observable, evidence-driven, simple and reversible, keep a reliable deterministic core, and use AI for judgment only where rules would be brittle. A release note derived from a retained record is a small, reversible projection of evidence the workflow already keeps — it belongs to the 'deliver → observe → evaluate actual outcome' part of the end state, and 'repository change'/'dependency release' are already named inputs. It does not conflict with any stated principle; the choice it replaces (no release boundary, no notes artifact, notes written afterwards) is a current design gap, not an enduring commitment. The main tension is with the documentation guide, which says maintained docs describe the intended system and history belongs in Git history — that argues for a regenerable derived artifact rather than a hand-tended changelog, which is the author's own anti-drift principle. Scope difference is fit-relevant, not a defect: notes for Nexus's own releases are self-application using this repo's record; notes for projects Nexus manages make it a workflow capability with per-project configuration.
steering: Anchor the notes to an explicit release boundary and range (a tag or named release event); today the project has none, so 'each release' is undefined and nothing could be derived.

Name which record supplies the entry text. Jira task summary/description is the most normalized human text for workflow-delivered changes; commit subjects here mix bare summaries, lower-case prefixes and HARN keys, so they read better as linkage than as prose.
Keep the artifact regenerated at release time rather than hand-maintained; that preserves the cannot-drift principle and stays consistent with the documentation guide's treatment of history.

Treat any adopted convention as forward-looking for new changes, and expect some merged changes to have no task key (63 of 233 subjects name a HARN key), so a source keyed only on Jira tasks would silently omit them.
Keep entries traceable to the record they came from (task key or PR reference) so a reader can check the note against what shipped.
constraints: No release event exists yet: `git tag` is empty, package.json is private at version 0.1.0, and .github contains only ci.yml — the idea presupposes a release boundary the project has not defined.
The merged change record is split across providers: Git subjects (mixed conventions), GitHub PR metadata/conversations, and Jira issues; no single existing artifact is 'the merged change record'.

Existing adapter capabilities cover Jira issue reads and GitHub PR reads, but the Git adapter's required capabilities (inspect, clone, fetch/resolve revision, pull, checkout, diff, push, read remote head) include no commit-range history read, so drawing the record from Git history would need a new read capability.

Per-change evidence already exists: CompleteTask retains taskKey, PR URL, reviewedHead, mergeRevision and check results (completionArtifact), and Deliver retains the PR identity and head — there is a record per change, but no aggregation and no release step.
The documentation guide excludes maintained history: 'Describe the system, not its implementation history... keep... ticket/PR references... in Git history, not in maintained docs or archives.'
